questions.question: What is a pattern guard in Java?
options: case Pattern p when condition: adds an extra condition to the pattern
A type of pattern that protects against NullPointerException
A clause that protects against compilation errors
An access modifier for patterns
explanations: Correct. A pattern guard uses the when keyword to add an additional condition to the pattern: case Pattern p when p.isValid().
It is not specifically for NPE.
It is not a compilation protection clause.
It is not an access modifier.

questions.question: What is a record pattern?
options: case Persona(String n, int e): decomposes a record into its components
A pattern that only works with abstract classes
A pattern for creating records
A way of serializing a record
explanations: Correct. A record pattern decomposes a record into its components directly in the case: case Persona(String name, int age).
It works with records, not abstract classes.
It is not for creating records.
It is not related to serialization.

questions.question: What is exhaustiveness in switch with pattern matching?
options: The compiler verifies that all possible cases are covered
An error that occurs from using too many case labels
A compiler warning about dead code
A restriction that limits the number of patterns
explanations: Correct. With sealed types or enums, the compiler can verify that all cases are covered and report if any are missing.
It is not about the number of cases.
It is not a warning about dead code.
There is no limit on the number of patterns.

questions.question: What is a sealed interface?
options: An interface that can only be implemented by a set of permitted classes
An interface with private methods
An interface that cannot have default methods
An interface with all static methods
explanations: Correct. A sealed interface restricts which classes can implement it through the permits clause.
It has nothing to do with private methods.
It can have default methods.
It has nothing to do with static methods.

questions.question: What are the permits in a sealed class?
options: The list of classes allowed to extend or implement the sealed class/interface
The access permissions of the methods
The exceptions the class can throw
The fields the class can have
explanations: Correct. The permits clause defines the specific classes (or interfaces) allowed to extend/implement the sealed class.
They have nothing to do with access permissions.
They have nothing to do with exceptions.
They have nothing to do with fields.
